A course in nine parts
Permitted Paths
Graph engineering for agents
You cannot remove the probability from the model. You can put structure around it. This course is about that structure, and about the three controls that make it.
Parts 0 to 8 · about 100 minutes with the instruments, 60 without
PART 0
Part 0 · the claim
An agent gets a small task: “Add a refund button to the order page.” It writes an endpoint, and the endpoint operates. Then a customer clicks the button two times, and gets two refunds.
No sentence in the prompt stopped it.
GE 00
PART 0
The claim of the course
Put the structure outside the model. Then the model makes a smaller number of decisions, and the system makes the other decisions.
Graph Engineering is the design of the graph in which an agent system operates.
GE 00
PART 0
Part 1 · the same question, five answers
Ask one model the same question five times
Order 1042 has an accepted payment. The email with the game key is in the send queue. “What is the status of order 1042?” Five new chats give five answers.
Chat 1
The order has been paid.
FAIL: not a status value
Chat 2
Status: PROCESSING
FAIL: not a permitted value
Chat 3
Awaiting fulfilment. The key email is queued.
FAIL: not a status value
Chat 4
Payment accepted, delivery pending.
FAIL: not a status value
Chat 5
PAID
PASS: code can use it
Each answer is defensible. A model gives a probability, not a lookup. All five are likely continuations of the same prompt.
Only one is usable. A system cannot act on an answer if it cannot predict the shape of the answer.
An agent does this in each turn. Which tool, which argument, when to stop: each decision can change the result.

PART 2
The same graph, as code
nodes
what operates
NODES = {   "classify":  (MODEL,  classify),   "answer":    (CODE,   answer),   "plan":      (AGENT,  make_plan),   "approve":   (PERSON, ask_approval),   "change":    (AGENT,  write_change),   "verify":    (CODE,   run_tests),   "summarise": (MODEL,  write_summary),   "escalate":  (PERSON, hand_to_person), }
edges
what comes next · no model here
EDGES = {   "classify": lambda s: "plan" if s.kind == "change" else "answer",   "plan":     lambda s: "approve",   "approve":  lambda s: "change" if s.approved else "escalate",   "change":   lambda s: "verify",   "verify":   lambda s: (       "summarise" if s.tests_pass else       "change" if s.attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS else       "escalate"), } TERMINAL = {"answer", "summarise", "escalate"}
The kind is in the contract. The colours are the colours of the drawing: model, code, agent, person.
An edge is a function of the state. No model selects the next node. That is control 1.
You can test an edge with no model. Give it a state. Examine the name of the next node.
Example code for teaching
PART 2
The state contract
state
what goes from node to node
@dataclass(frozen=True) class RunState:     run_id:     str     request:    str     kind:       Literal["question", "change"] | None = None     plan:       str | None = None     approved:   bool = False     attempts:   int = 0     tests_pass: bool = False     facts:      tuple[Fact, ...] = ()     # a node does not change the state. It gives the next state.     def with_(self, **kw) -> "RunState":         return replace(self, **kw) Node = Callable[[RunState], RunState]
Why frozen
Each node has the same shape: a state in, a new state out. No other data goes across the edge of a node.
Why small
If a field is not in this class, no edge can use it to select a path. A small state gives a small number of possible paths.
What you get
You can keep each state, compare it and use it again. A failed run becomes a test: load the state before the bad step, and do that one node.
attempts is in the state. Thus the edge counts, not the model.
PART 2
The runtime is fourteen lines
run
obeys the edges · counts · writes the trace
def run(state, start="classify", max_steps=24):     node = start     for step in range(max_steps):         kind, fn = NODES[node]         began = time.monotonic()         state = fn(state)         # 1 · a model can operate only here         trace.write(state.run_id, step, node, kind, state, began)         if node in TERMINAL:             return state         if node == "verify" and not state.tests_pass:             state = state.with_(attempts=state.attempts + 1)         node = EDGES[node](state)     # 2 · code selects the path     return hand_to_person(state)  # 3 · no end: a person gets the run
A framework is not necessary at the start. The runtime obeys the edges, counts the attempts, and writes a trace for each step.
1 · One place for the model
The model operates in a node. It operates in no other line.
2 · Code selects the path
The edge reads the state and gives the next node. The attempt limit is in the edge.
3 · A person at the end
After the maximum number of steps, a person gets the run.
Example code for teaching
PART 2
Part 2 · the four parts: nodes, edges, state, control
A node is not always a model call
code
Fixed step
Code. No model.
Predictable: fully
model
Model step
One model call with no tools.
Predictable: not fully
agent
Agent step
A model that uses tools in a loop.
Predictable: less than a model step
code
Verifier
A check of the work of a different node.
Predictable: fully, if it is code
person
Person step
A person gives approval or rejects.
Predictable: fully, as a point in the path
A test for a node. Write what the node does in one sentence with no “and”. If you cannot do this, divide the node.
Edges. A fixed edge: node B always comes after node A. A conditional edge: a function reads the state and gives the name of the next node.
State and control. The state goes from node to node. The control is the runtime: it enforces the edges and counts the attempts.
GE 02 · in the course, you give a type to each node
PART 2
The default is one loop with a strict verifier
When a specific problem occurs, add a graph. One clear “yes” in the right column is sufficient.
Question about the task
One loop is sufficient
Use a graph
Can you write the task as one instruction?
Yes
No. The task goes from one role to a different role.
Does each step use the same model and tools?
Yes
No. Some steps use a small model, some a large model.
Are some steps independent?
No
Yes, and they can operate at the same time
Who makes the decision that the result is good?
A check in the loop, for example the tests
A node that did not write the result
What must occur after a failure of one step?
Try again
Isolate the failure. The other work continues.
Who must read the record of the path?
Only your team
A person outside the team must see which step occurred
Three good causes for a new node: specialization, parallel work and independent verification. Do not use a graph if the task is open and you cannot give its steps before the run. If all the steps are code, a script is sufficient.
GE 02
PART 2
Part 3 · which graph do you mean?
Four things have the name “graph”
control
Execution graph
What comes next?
Nodes are units of work.
The design is permanent. Each run is one pass.
data
Knowledge graph
What is in the domain?
Nodes are entities: a customer, a file.
Continues across runs.
data
Context graph
What occurred in this run?
Nodes are steps, tool calls and records.
Permanent. Each run adds a trace.
control
Procedural graph
Which paths are permitted?
Nodes are steps of a procedure.
Permanent. Many runs use it again.
Control and data. A procedural graph is data that a harness loads. An execution graph is code that the runtime enforces.
Two causes of confusion. GraphRAG is about data, not control. A context graph is a graph of traces. It is not the context window of a model.

GE 03 §2 · the cycle
PART 3
2
Part 4 · control 2 · the ontology
A prompt asks the model to obey a rule. An ontology makes the rule a check for each result.
In part 1, you asked for the status of order 1042 five times. The correct status is PAID. An ontology gives the permitted words. The model suggests a result, and the ontology rejects each result that is not permitted.
GE 04 §1–3
PART 4
An ontology that code can use
ontology
the permitted results
class OrderStatus(str, Enum):     PENDING   = "PENDING"     PAID      = "PAID"     FULFILLED = "FULFILLED"     REFUNDED  = "REFUNDED"     CANCELLED = "CANCELLED"
RULES = [   Rule("LV-1", "an order has at most one refund",     lambda f, r: count(f, "refund", order_id=r.order_id) <= 1),   Rule("LV-2", "a refund pays the customer of its order",     lambda f, r: r.customer_id == order(f, r.order_id).customer_id),   Rule("LV-3", "only a PAID or FULFILLED order can be refunded",     lambda f, r: order(f, r.order_id).status in REFUNDABLE), ]
Start with the enumeration
Five permitted values. Four of the five answers of part 1 are now not possible.
Give each rule an id
The prompt sentence “do not refund an order two times” became LV-1. A gate uses the id, and a trace records it.
Keep the rules as data
A person can read the list. A test can run the list. You can count the list in the trace.
Control 2 · GE 04 · example code for teaching
PART 4
Part 4 · control 3 · the gates
Two gates around each tool call
the agent loop
in words
while the task is not complete:     proposal = the model suggests a tool call     # GATE 1: is the shape of the call correct?     result = the tool makes a result,              with no change to data     # GATE 2: does the result obey the ontology?     record the change,     or send the cause back to the model
Gate 1 · input
Before the tool operates. The shape of the call: types, ranges, necessary fields. It reads only the call.
Gate 2 · output
After the tool operates. The sense of the result: cardinality, roles, agreement with the state of the world.
The rule · a pure agent
The agent calculates and gives a result. It does not change the world during the loop. Thus you can reject a result and lose nothing.
GE 04 · from a source: Frank Coyle
PART 4
Gate 1: is the shape of the call correct?
gate 1
before the tool operates · reads only the call
class RefundCall(BaseModel):     model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")     order_id:     int     amount_cents: PositiveInt     reason:       Literal["duplicate", "faulty", "goodwill"]     currency:     Literal["EUR", "GBP", "USD"] = "EUR"
TOOL_SCHEMAS = {"refund": RefundCall, "search_notes": SearchCall}
def gate_1(name: str, args: dict) -> Result:     schema = TOOL_SCHEMAS.get(name)     if schema is None:         return Reject("GATE 1", f"no tool has the name {name!r}")     try:         return Accept(schema.model_validate(args))     except ValidationError as e:         return Reject("GATE 1", readable(e))
Low cost, large effect
No database is necessary. The gate stops a call to a tool that does not exist, and an argument that the model invented.
Do not permit extra fields
One line. Without it, the system ignores force=true today, and obeys it after a person adds that parameter.
Write the cause for a reader
The text goes back to the model. “amount_cents must be more than 0” corrects the next attempt.
Control 3, first half · example code for teaching
PART 4
Gate 2: does the result obey the ontology?
gate 2
after the tool operates · reads the facts
def gate_2(call, result, facts) -> Result:     for rule in RULES:         if not rule.holds(facts, result):             return Reject("GATE 2", rule.id, rule.text)     return Accept(result)
# the check and the commit: one transaction with db.transaction() as tx:     facts   = tx.facts_for(call.order_id)     verdict = gate_2(call, result, facts)     if verdict.rejected:         tx.rollback()   # no data is lost         return back_to_model(verdict.text)     tx.apply(result)
It reads the facts
Gate 1 cannot know that order 1042 has a refund. Gate 2 reads the call, the result, the ontology and the current facts.
the database
LV-1
ALTER TABLE refund   ADD CONSTRAINT one_refund_per_order   UNIQUE (order_id);
Make each cardinality rule a constraint in the database also. Then the rule continues to operate if the gate has a defect.

PART 4
The second refund, and the three places that stop it
the model
Suggests a call
refund(  order_id=1042,  amount=4999)
gate 1 · PASS
The shape is correct
The call has the correct fields. An invented argument stops here.
the tool
Makes a result
A refund record, with no change to data. The agent is pure.
gate 2 · FAIL
Rule LV-1 rejects it
The order has a refund. The transaction rolls back. The cause goes to the model.
the database
Refuses the insert
If gate 2 has a defect, the unique constraint stops the second refund.
One rule, in three places that the model cannot ignore. The prompt had the rule one time, in the one place that the model can ignore.

PART 4
Part 5 · what the system knows
All teams can buy the same models. The model is not the difference.
Control plane
Which steps are permitted, and in which sequence.
the permitted next step
Data plane
The agent runtime: models, tools and the calls they make.
a trace of each step
facts, types and rules
Intelligence plane
The ontology, the knowledge graph and the traces.
The difference between two agent systems is what each system knows about its own domain. That knowledge lives in a layer of its own.
Read the arrows. The control plane gives the path. The data plane does the work and writes a trace. The intelligence plane keeps the traces and gives back the facts, the types and the rules that the three controls use.
Teaching model. The word “plane” comes from network engineering. The three planes are a way to sort the parts of a design. They are not a standard. The talk gives two planes; the notes add the data plane as a name for the agent runtime.
GE 05 §2
PART 5
How one run makes the next run better
The intelligence plane is a loop. Each run goes around it one time.
1 · Ontology
Types, values and rules. Each rule has an id.
2 · Gate
Each result of the run gets a check against the rules.
3 · Trace
One row for each step: the node, the rule id, PASS or FAIL.
4 · Query
Which rule gives FAIL most? Which fact was absent?
5 · correct the rule, or add the fact that was absent
The amber arrow is the important one. If the trace does not go back into the ontology, the system makes the same error in the next run.
The rule id carries the lesson. A trace with no rule id is a log. You can read it, but you cannot count it. The next slide gives the row and the query.
GE 05
PART 5
The trace: one row for each step
the row
written by the runtime
trace.write({   "run_id":     run_id,   "step":       step,   "node":       node,   "kind":       kind,   "inputs":     redact(before),   "output":     redact(after),   "tool_calls": calls,   "gate":       verdict.gate,     # GATE 1, GATE 2   "rule":       verdict.rule_id,  # LV-1, LV-3   "result":     verdict.name,     # PASS or FAIL   "model":      model_id,   "latency_ms": ms, })
the query
which rule gives FAIL most?
SELECT rule, count(*) AS fails   FROM trace  WHERE result = 'FAIL'    AND ts > now() - interval '7 days'  GROUP BY rule ORDER BY fails DESC;
Record the gate and the rule
The three amber fields make the query possible. With no rule id, you have a log that you cannot count.
Remove private data first
Make the decision about what the trace can keep before you write the first row.

GE 08 · this course is an execution graph, and you are a run
PART 8
The sequence in which to make it
Each step is useful alone, and each step makes the next step easier. Do not start with the graph.
When
What you make
How you know that it operates
Hour 1
Find one rule in one prompt. Make it an enumeration and a validator.
Measure the variation before and after, with the procedure of part 1.
Day 1
Gate 1 on each tool: a schema for each call, no extra fields.
Calls with an incorrect shape do not get to your tools.
Week 1
Make the agent pure. Add Gate 2 and the database constraints.
A rejected result causes a rollback and no other change.
Week 2
Write the trace: one row for each step, with the rule id and PASS or FAIL.
A query answers “which rule gives FAIL most?”
Week 3
Now the execution graph: move the sequence into NODES and EDGES.
The edge functions have tests that use no model.
Month 2
Use the trace: correct the rules that give FAIL most, add the absent facts.
The same task needs a smaller number of attempts.
If you do only hour 1, you moved one decision from the model to the system. That is the course.
Controls 2 and 3 first. Control 1 last.
PART 8
The course in one line
Fewer decisions for the model. Fewer results that are valid. A check before each change. And a layer that keeps what each run learned.
